title: From Mardaani to Delhi Crime: Hindi Cinema's Women Cops Take Charge
excerpt: Rani Mukerji's franchise completed an unprecedented hattrick of hits, while streaming turned Shefali Shah, Sonakshi Sinha and Raveena Tandon into television's most compelling investigators.
body:
• Rediff's Sukanya Verma spotlights Hindi cinema's new wave of women in uniform, from Kareena Kapoor Khan's "cop who wears lipstick" in Daayra to Rani Mukerji's Shivani Shivaji Roy.
  • Mardaani 3 closed its 2026 theatrical run at about ₹77 crore — the franchise's best — completing the first hattrick of hits for a female-cop series in 113 years of Hindi cinema.
  • Streaming drove the shift: Delhi Crime, Dahaad, Aranyak, Kohrra and Brown gave women investigators sustained screen time after Netflix's 2016 India entry rewrote the economics of risk.
  • Actresses say the draw is complexity, not the uniform: flawed protagonists whose vulnerability and competence coexist.

In early 2026, Rani Mukerji's Mardaani 3 closed its theatrical run earning about ₹77 crore — the highest-grossing film in the 12-year-old franchise's history. It made the Mardaani series the only female-cop franchise to succeed in 113 years of Hindi cinema. For Rediff film critic Sukanya Verma, the milestone is part of a wider turn: from Kareena Kapoor Khan's "cop who wears lipstick" in Daayra to Mukerji's relentless Shivani Shivaji Roy, Bollywood's portrayals of female police officers have grown more powerful — and more nuanced.

A long history of one-offs

Women in uniform have appeared in Indian cinema since at least the 1980s. They just never stayed long enough to change anything. Hema Malini wore the khaki in Andhaa Kaanoon (1983); Rekha headlined Phool Bane Angaray (1991). In the South, Vijayashanti built something more sustained in Telugu cinema through the late 1980s and 1990s — an action-heroine identity that earned her the nickname "Lady Amitabh." Tabu turned the investigating officer into a morally complicated figure in the Drishyam franchise; Priyanka Chopra Jonas played a district superintendent in Jai Gangaajal (2016). Each portrayal was remarkable; each remained an island.

The reason was economic. Indian cinema's formula was organised around a simple equation: audiences came for the male star. From Amitabh Bachchan in Zanjeer to Ajay Devgn in Singham, the cop was imagined as a masculine force imposing order through brute strength. "Even if a woman-centric film does well, there is no comparison to a man-centric film doing well," says Brown director Abhinay Deo. "We're talking about ticket sales and the film scenario, until OTT came along."

The OTT cascade

Netflix's 2016 India entry, followed by JioHotstar, ZEE5, SonyLIV and Prime Video, changed the economics that had limited storytelling to familiar tropes. "Prime time has changed to my time, and OTT has brought about that change," says Devendra Deshpande, CEO of Friday Filmworks.

Delhi Crime was the proof of concept. Shefali Shah's calm, razor-sharp DCP Vartika Chaturvedi won India its first International Emmy for Best Drama Series in 2020; a third season streamed in November 2025, and the show became the most-watched in 10 countries on Netflix.

"Even today, when I wear that uniform, I get goosebumps. Every single time I wear it, I stand differently."

— Shefali Shah, on playing DCP Vartika Chaturvedi in Delhi Crime

The cascade that followed was quick. Sonakshi Sinha's Anjali Bhaati in Dahaad placed a small-town Rajasthani officer at the centre of a serial-killer investigation tangled with caste, gender and institutional prejudice. Raveena Tandon's Kasturi Dogra juggled a murder mystery with family pressures in Aranyak; Bhumi Pednekkar's Rita Ferreira was the flawed heart of Daldal; Mona Singh's Baljit Kaur anchored Kohrra; Kareena Kapoor Khan carried a cold case in England in The Buckingham Murders; Deepika Padukone entered Rohit Shetty's cop universe in Singham Again. In June 2026, Karisma Kapoor returned in Brown as Rita Brown, a recovering alcoholic detective with the Kolkata police.

Vulnerability as the point

What connects these women is a proposition once foreign to Indian mainstream storytelling: their vulnerability and competence coexist. "Portraying authority on screen isn't about volume or aggression. It's about stillness, conviction and knowing exactly when to push and when to hold back," Sinha says. "With Anjali, her flaws and vulnerabilities don't take away from her strength, they define it."

Impact and analysis

The creative change had to survive the commercial one, and Mardaani 3 is the strongest evidence it did: when the first film released in 2014, Mukerji's Shivani Roy — a mainstream Hindi action heroine, neither young nor glamorous — carried the film's weight alone. The franchise survived a six-year gap and returned in 2026 to its best numbers yet.

Diaspora angle

Streaming has made these performances global by default: Delhi Crime topped charts in 10 countries, and NRI audiences have discovered Indian crime drama on the same platforms that carry their Bollywood tentpoles.

What's next

Rohit Shetty has confirmed a standalone film for Deepika Padukone's Lady Singham, and Kareena Kapoor Khan's Daayra will test whether the theatrical audience keeps growing.
